claims.text: Enhanced free-energy sampling calibrated with high-fidelity ab initio parameters can reliably determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
High-entropy alloys near their melting point can exist as highly configurationally disordered solid solutions.
The free-energy balance of high-entropy alloys is sensitive to temperature near melting.
Metadynamics or parallel-tempering molecular dynamics can map the free-energy landscape near melting in high-entropy alloys.
Parameters derived from first-principles calculations can calibrate computational models of high-entropy-alloy thermodynamics and phase evolution.
Constant-composition and constant-pressure simulations can mimic calorimetric and in situ imaging conditions near melting.
A solid-to-liquid transition produces discontinuities or inflection points in the mapped free-energy landscape.
Enhanced sampling accelerates rare thermodynamic fluctuations during melting.
Enhanced sampling enables detailed mapping of free-energy changes during melting.
Free-energy discontinuities or cusps can identify melting temperature, latent heat, fusion entropy, and melting volume change.
The calculated free-energy profiles will show a sharp transition feature at a specific temperature.
The simulated transition features will correlate directly with experimental melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change.
The proposed method will achieve accuracy within the experimental error margins of high-resolution calorimetry or in situ neutron imaging.
The proposed method will be more computationally efficient than traditional simulation methods.
Conventional molecular dynamics, Monte Carlo, and CALPHAD approaches generally trade accuracy for efficiency or require extensive resources without fully capturing HEA melting behavior.
The approach is applicable across a broad range of high-entropy-alloy compositions whose high-temperature behavior is governed predominantly by configurational entropy.
Strong local ordering or unexpected intermetallic formation may limit the method's accuracy by altering the free-energy landscape.
Force-field calibration and convergence of enhanced-sampling simulations are important sources of uncertainty in complex high-entropy alloys.
The quantitative relationship between simulated transition features and latent heat or volume change may vary with composition and local ordering.
